name: Cabernet Franc

lines.s10: Cabernet Franc is the fragrant red of the Loire: raspberry, violet and pencil shavings on a light, fresh frame.
lines.s20: Cabernet Franc is the red of Chinon and Bourgueil in the Loire, and the partner of Merlot in Saint-Émilion. It is lighter and more perfumed than Cabernet Sauvignon, with raspberry, violet and a leafy edge of green pepper.
lines.s45: Cabernet Franc came first of the two Cabernets, and its home today is the Loire Valley, in Chinon, Bourgueil and Saumur-Champigny. It tastes of raspberry and redcurrant, with violet and a streak of pencil shavings and green bell pepper. It is medium in body, bright and fresh, with fine tannin. The Loire raises it with little new oak, while Argentina and California often make it darker, riper and rounder. Serve it a little cool, with roast chicken, charcuterie or goat's cheese. Crossed by chance with Sauvignon Blanc, it gave the world Cabernet Sauvignon, and it is a parent of Merlot too.
lines.sale: Cabernet Franc is a red with the freshness of a white: raspberry, violet and a cool, leafy snap. Serve it a little cool with the roast chicken or the charcuterie.

glass.lead: Raspberry and redcurrant with violet, pencil shavings and green bell pepper, on a medium body with bright acidity and fine tannin.

ladder.where: Chinon, Bourgueil and Saumur-Champigny; the Finger Lakes and Ontario
Saint-Émilion, Long Island, Virginia and Hawke's Bay
Mendoza, Napa Valley, Tuscany's coast and Stellenbosch

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium plus to high, tannin medium to medium plus, fine and chalky, alcohol moderate, body medium.

old.where: The Loire's Chinon, Bourgueil and Saumur-Champigny; Bordeaux's Right Bank
old.glass: Tends to be light to medium and brisk: raspberry, redcurrant and violet with pencil shavings and green bell pepper, high acidity and moderate alcohol. On the Right Bank it is usually blended, and adds perfume to Merlot.
old.cellar: In the Loire, usually bottled alone and raised in steel, concrete or old casks with little new oak; gravel gives lighter wines, limestone slopes firmer ones.

new.where: The Finger Lakes, Long Island, Virginia, Ontario, Mendoza, California and Chile
new.glass: Typically riper and fuller: black cherry and plum with roasted pepper, softer acidity, more alcohol and vanilla from new oak in Mendoza and California. New York and Ontario stay closer to the Loire, with raspberry and a leafy edge.
new.cellar: Often bottled under the grape's own name, or blended with Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot; warmer regions tend to pick riper and use more new French oak.

contrast.why: The Loire is cool and northerly, so the grape ripens only just, keeping high acidity and its leafy edge. Warm, sunny New World sites ripen the green note away. The Loire labels the village, the New World the grape.
contrast.blur: The Finger Lakes and Ontario are cool enough to taste like the Loire, while Tuscany's coast and Villány in Hungary make dark, ripe wines, as warm years do in Chinon.
contrast.call: Raspberry, pencil shavings and high acidity at moderate alcohol lean Loire; black cherry, roasted pepper and vanilla on a rounder body lean New World.

service.temp: 54 to 59 degrees Fahrenheit, 12 to 15 degrees Celsius, lightly cool; a fuller, oaked wine a few degrees warmer.
service.glass: A Bordeaux glass; a Burgundy bowl suits a light, perfumed Loire wine.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary for a young Loire red; an old Chinon may be decanted gently off its sediment.
service.age: Light Loire wines within three or four years; Chinon and Bourgueil from limestone slopes five to fifteen.

with.why: a light body and bright acidity suit white meat
fresh acidity balances the richness: the Loire's own match
the wine's freshness meets the cheese's tang
a cool, light red with fine tannin can take firm fish

labels.means: Loire place names for reds made almost wholly from Cabernet Franc: the label names the village.
The old local name for Cabernet Franc in the Loire.
The grape's traditional name in Saint-Émilion and Pomerol, where it is blended with Merlot.

guest.q: Is this the same grape as Cabernet Sauvignon?
guest.a: No, it is one of its parents. Cabernet Franc is lighter and more fragrant, with raspberry and violet where Cabernet Sauvignon has cassis, and its tannin is gentler.

guest.q: Why does it taste a little of green pepper?
guest.a: That leafy note belongs to the grape, and a cool climate keeps it. In a ripe year it sits quietly behind the raspberry, and wines from warmer places show less of it.

guest.q: Should a red really be served cool?
guest.a: A light Loire red, yes. A slight chill lifts its fruit and freshness, and too much warmth makes it taste flat. It should feel cool in the mouth, not cold.

compare.tell: Cabernet Sauvignon is darker and firmer, with cassis, cedar and heavier tannin; Cabernet Franc is lighter and more perfumed, with raspberry and violet.
Merlot is plummier, rounder and softer, with no pencil shavings; Cabernet Franc is leaner and brighter, with a leafy edge.
Carmenère, its offspring, is darker, fuller and softer, with soy and paprika; Cabernet Franc is lighter, with redcurrant, pencil shavings and higher acidity.

cards.front: Cabernet Franc: its villages in the Loire, and its two local names?
cards.back: Chinon, Bourgueil, Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil and Saumur-Champigny. It is Breton in the Loire and Bouchet in Saint-Émilion and Pomerol.

cards.front: Cabernet Franc blind: the Loire or the New World, what tips it?
cards.back: Raspberry, pencil shavings, green bell pepper and high acidity at moderate alcohol lean Loire. Black cherry, roasted pepper, vanilla and a rounder body lean Mendoza or California.

cards.front: Which three well known red grapes have Cabernet Franc as a parent?
cards.back: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Carmenère. The cross with Sauvignon Blanc that gave Cabernet Sauvignon was shown by DNA work published in 1997.

questions.q: Two glasses of Cabernet Franc are poured blind. The first is pale ruby, with raspberry, pencil shavings and green bell pepper, high acidity and moderate alcohol. The second is darker, with black cherry, roasted pepper and vanilla. Which pair of origins fits, in that order?
questions.exp: Tart raspberry, a green edge, high acidity and moderate alcohol say the cool Loire. Darker, riper fruit with vanilla from new oak says a warm, sunny New World site such as Mendoza.

questions.q: A guest orders a young Chinon with the charcuterie on a warm evening and asks how you will serve it. What do you do?
opts: Serve it lightly cool, straight into the glass
Decant it for an hour at room temperature
Pour it over ice in a white wine glass
Stand the bottle near the kitchen to warm
questions.exp: A light Loire red shows well at 54 to 59 degrees Fahrenheit, 12 to 15 degrees Celsius, and seldom needs decanting. Warmth flattens it, and ice would dilute it.

questions.q: A guest sees the word Breton beside a red on a Loire list and asks which grape it is. What do you tell him?
questions.exp: Breton is the old Loire name for Cabernet Franc, the grape of Chinon and Bourgueil. Cabernet Sauvignon is allowed in Chinon only as a small share, and Breton is not its name.

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it. TASTE.world reads old: the entry agrees that the Loire and the Right Bank are the grape's home, and sets New York, Ontario, Mendoza and California beside them as the styles a guest now meets under the grape's own name.
The Codex's records on Cabernet Franc read true and nothing here departs from them; say is the Court's own respelling.

The origin is left as the Cabernet that came first, with no birthplace: the reference works point to the Basque Country and the sources read do not agree, so the entry states only the parentage, which the Davis work of 1997 and the paper of 2009 settle.
The name Breton is given with no story: the abbot of the legend is a hypothesis in every source read.

The ladder puts the Finger Lakes and Ontario on the cool rung with the Loire, as the Court's grid reads Chinon and Bourgueil cool; New York's wine body calls the Finger Lakes style the more leafy and Long Island's the riper.
Mendoza's riper, darker style stands on tasting reports read through search and on the Codex's own region record, which names the grape there; no body of Argentina's was read for it.
Grilled redfish is the one dish from the Creole table: the Loire itself pours its light reds cool with river fish.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.

checked.verdict: Sound after ten fixes over two rounds. The parentage, Breton and Bouchet, the two soils of Chinon, Cabernet d'Anjou and the warm style of Villány were confirmed; the blur left out the warm Old World exceptions, two lines hid a family word and one misheard a pepper, one explanation claimed what no source shows, and one food line said what the Codex's pairing data asks never to be said.
changed: lines.s45: while Argentina and California make it darker, riper and rounder now reads while Argentina and California often make it darker, riper and rounder. An unhedged clause on the New World said aloud as a rule: often, as the brief asks of a typical style.
worlds.contrast.old.where: Villány's Cabernet Franc is ripe, dark and full, nothing like the brisk style the Old World glass describes; it moves to the blur as the warm exception.

worlds.contrast.blur: The blur named only warm years in the Loire. Villány, Hungary's warmest district, makes Cabernet Franc fuller than the Loire's and without its green edge, and the Tuscan coast is on the entry's own warm rung: both are the warm Old World the blur must admit.

worlds.contrast.new.glass: New York and Ontario often stay close to the Loire, red fruited and leafy now reads New York and Ontario often stay close to the Loire, with raspberry and a leafy edge. Red fruited is a family word in disguise; the fruit is named.

compare, the Cabernet Sauvignon tell: Cabernet Franc is lighter, red fruited and more perfumed now reads Cabernet Franc is lighter and more perfumed, with raspberry and violet. Red fruited again, a family word in disguise; raspberry and violet are named, and the Cabernet Sauvignon pilot carries neither.

compare, the Carmenère tell: The tell gave roasted pepper to Carmenère, but this entry's own warm rung lists roasted red pepper, and it gave raspberry to Cabernet Franc, which the Carmenère entry lists among its own notes. Soy and paprika, and redcurrant and pencil shavings, now part them.

lines.s20: with raspberry, violet and a leafy, peppery edge now reads with raspberry, violet and a leafy edge of green pepper. A leafy, peppery edge is heard at the table as black pepper; the grape's note is green bell pepper, as the reviewed profile and the grid read have it.

questions[1].exp: at 54 to 59 degrees Fahrenheit, 12 to 15 Celsius, and seldom needs decanting now reads at 54 to 59 degrees Fahrenheit, 12 to 15 degrees Celsius, and seldom needs decanting. The service form: degrees Celsius with the word degrees.

food.with, charcuterie: The Codex's pairing data asks that acid or tannin never be described as stripping fat from the mouth; acidity cuts the fat says just that. The line now speaks of balance, an impression.

questions[2].exp: Cabernet Sauvignon is allowed in Chinon only as a small share, and has no such local name now reads Cabernet Sauvignon is allowed in Chinon only as a small share, and Breton is not its name. Has no such local name claimed more than can be shown: Cabernet Sauvignon has old Bordeaux names of its own, Vidure among them. What is true and enough is that Breton is not its name.
open: Chilli flake sits under herbal, as the reviewed profile lists it beside jalapeño; spice would be its truer family, but the entry carries no other spice note and a group needs two.

The ten second line calls the frame light where the profile and the forty five second line say medium in body. Light is the table's word for Chinon set beside Cabernet Sauvignon, and the Old World glass says light to medium; left.

The Blaufränkisch entry of chunk g8 parts its grape from Cabernet Franc by black cherry and brighter acidity; this entry lists black cherry and acidity of medium plus to high. A note for that chunk's reader; not edited here.
